evidence.title: An Experimental Investigation of the Relationship between AI-Human Workflow Design and Legal Liability for Radiologists: The Erroneous-Change Penalty and Omission Bias
evidence.outcome: Perceived radiologist liability when AI error rates (FDR/FOR) disclosed to participants
evidence.effect: Providing participants with AI error rates, including FDR (p=0.0038) or FOR (p=0.0035), reduced perceived liability; radiologist awareness of error rates did not significantly change liability.
evidence.quote: Double-read workflows (p<0.0001), documenting initial interpretations (p=0.0125), and providing participants with AI error rates, including the FDR (p=0.0038) or FOR (p=0.0035), reduced perceived liability.

evidence.title: Locally calibrated error rates improve interpretability of AI scores and influence radiologist decision-making
evidence.outcome: Radiologist recall decisions and confidence when FDR/FOR shown alongside AI scores versus scores alone
evidence.effect: Recall was higher with AI scores alone than with FDR/FOR (OR 2.9, 95% CI 1.331-6.417, p=0.0077); confidence was higher when FDR/FOR were provided, especially at intermediate scores.
evidence.quote: Confidence followed a U-shaped relationship with score and was higher when FDR/FOR were provided, particularly at intermediate scores.

evidence.outcome: Share of public summaries reporting a canonical performance metric
evidence.effect: A canonical performance metric was stated for 52.3% of decisions.
evidence.quote: Clinical data were stated for 70.6%, a canonical performance metric for 52.3%, multisite evaluation for 42.7%, and prospective or reader studies for 16.8%.

evidence.title: Generalizability of FDA-Approved AI-Enabled Medical Devices for Clinical Use
evidence.outcome: Reporting of discriminatory performance metrics in public summaries
evidence.effect: Reported in 200 summaries; sensitivity 183 devices (36.2%), specificity 176 (34.9%), AUC 82 (16.2%).
evidence.quote: Discriminatory performance metrics were reported in 200 of the available summaries (sensitivity: 183 devices [36.2%]; specificity: 176 devices [34.9%]; area under the curve: 82 devices [16.2%]).

commentary.bottom_line: Two simulated US studies suggest that showing AI error rates (false discovery and false omission rates) may change radiologist recall decisions and confidence and may lower perceived radiologist liability, but no study tested reporting at several operating points or with confidence intervals, and none measured patient outcomes. The recommendation rests mainly on professional consensus and on descriptive evidence that performance reporting is often missing.

perspectives.view: Both tests are level 4 simulations with surrogate outcomes. One measured perceived liability among 2,347 participants, and the other measured recall and confidence among 21 radiologists. Neither tested sensitivity, specificity, operating points, or confidence intervals as the recommendation specifies. Indirectness and the small reader sample lead to very low certainty.

Among 21 radiologists, recall was higher with AI scores alone than with error rates shown (OR 2.9, 95% CI 1.331-6.417). The study did not report whether the extra recalls were correct or unnecessary. Without accuracy against a reference standard, the effect on missed cancers or false alarms remains unknown.

Radiologists reported higher confidence when error rates were displayed, especially at intermediate AI scores. This suggests that context may matter most where the score is ambiguous. The test used retrospective replay, so display burden, fidelity, and use in live reading workflows were not assessed.

FDA draft guidance asks for a description of device performance metrics, yet a canonical performance metric appeared in 52.3% of 1,491 510(k) and De Novo public summaries. A vignette study found that disclosing error rates reduced perceived radiologist liability, which may bear on malpractice exposure, though perceived liability differs from legal findings.

Neither test reported enrollment of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and neither examined subgroup performance reporting. The evidence cannot show whether metrics reported to users reflect performance in these populations.

In the vignette study, participants who were given AI error rates judged radiologists less liable. This suggests that disclosure may shape how the public assigns responsibility. No study asked whether patients received the information, understood it, or could reach a clinician to discuss it.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested whether reporting sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values at multiple operating points with confidence intervals improves clinician accuracy, calibration of trust, or patient outcomes in live clinical use. Prospective or randomized comparisons of reporting formats that measure diagnostic accuracy against a reference standard across specialties beyond radiology would address this.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and both were US simulations. Whether reported metrics hold, or are interpreted the same way, in settings that serve these populations remains untested.
